Buddhism. Buddhism is a major world religion and philosophical system founded in ancient India by Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, in the sixth to fifth centuries BCE. Focusing on spiritual development and the attainment of insight into the true nature of reality, it teaches that existence is characterized by suffering, or dukkha, which arises from ignorance and craving but can be overcome through ethical conduct, meditation, and wisdom to attain Nirvana—the ultimate liberation. Unlike religions centered on divine beings or revelation, Buddhism is fundamentally a practical path of self-transformation grounded in rational inquiry and personal experience. Starting in India, it spread throughout Asia, adapting to local cultures while maintaining core doctrines, becoming one of the world's major religions with over five hundred million adherents. Buddhism's emphasis on compassion, mental discipline, and philosophical sophistication has made it influential far beyond Asia in modern psychology, philosophy, and spiritual practice.

The Four Noble Truths form the foundation: suffering exists, suffering has causes rooted in craving and ignorance, suffering can end, and there is a path to end suffering. The Noble Eightfold Path—right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration—provides the practical guide to liberation, divided into wisdom, ethical conduct, and mental discipline.

Dukkha, or suffering and unsatisfactoriness, is not pessimism but a diagnosis. All conditioned phenomena involve some form of suffering due to impermanence and lack of an enduring self. The Anatta, or non-self, doctrine rejects the Vedic concept of a permanent, eternal soul called Atman. It teaches instead that what we call self is a constantly changing assemblage of five aggregates.

Buddhism explicitly rejects the authority of the Vedas and the Brahmin-led ritual system, attacking the Vedic caste system as unjust. It offers an alternative path to liberation open to all, regardless of birth caste, creating the monastic community, or sangha, as an alternative to brahminical priesthood.

Buddhism develops sophisticated theories of epistemology, logic, metaphysics, and ethics. Later Buddhist philosophers engaged in rigorous debate with Hindu and other philosophical schools. The Pali Canon, also called the Tripitaka or "Three Baskets," comprises the Vinaya of monastic rules, the Sutta of discourses, and the Abhidhamma of philosophical analysis, representing an encyclopedic philosophical system.

Theravada is the oldest surviving school, prominent in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, emphasizing monastic practice and individual enlightenment. Mahayana, popular in East Asia, emphasizes the bodhisattva ideal—postponing one's own Nirvana to help all sentient beings achieve liberation. Vajrayana, or Tibetan Buddhism, incorporates esoteric practices, tantric rituals, and the idea that enlightenment can be achieved in one lifetime.

Buddhism's rise and eventual decline in India yet flourishing in Asia represents one of history's great religious transformations. In India, it directly challenged brahminical authority and the Vedic worldview, offering an alternative path to liberation grounded in reason and practice rather than ritual and caste. The patronage of the Mauryan Emperor Ashoka the Great in the third century BCE, who converted to Buddhism and sent missionaries throughout Asia, was crucial to its spread. The adaptation of Buddhism to different Asian contexts—Sanskrit philosophy in Kashmir, meditation mysticism in Tibet, Pure Land devotionalism in East Asia, and Zen simplicity in Japan—demonstrates its flexibility while maintaining core doctrines. In modern times, Buddhism has resonated in the West as a philosophical and spiritual discipline compatible with scientific naturalism, making it influential in psychology, cognitive science, and contemporary spirituality.
